prompt: On a shared 5 V rail the servo stalls and the processor reboots mid-move. What is the mechanism?
options: Commutation noise couples into the module and corrupts the running firmware
The PWM pin sinks the stall current and drags the chip's supply down with it
About 0.9 A across the cable and connector resistance sags the regulator's input past its headroom

prompt: A beginner pushes the servo's 3-pin plug on backwards. What does the GND / V+ / SIG order guarantee?
options: Reversing swaps the two outer pins, so power never lands on the signal
The connector is keyed, so it cannot physically go on backwards
The series resistor absorbs the reversed supply until the fuse trips

prompt: You have a standard-size MG996R in a drawer and it fits the same 3-pin header. Why is it out of bounds on this board?
options: Its plug uses a different pin order, so V+ would land on the signal pin
It stalls near 2.5 A, well past the 0.9 A worst case the fuse, the capacitor and the trace widths were proven against
It needs a 12 V supply, and this board's terminal is 5 V only

prompt: The 1.5 A PTC is out of stock and a 1.0 A hold part from the same family is on the shelf. What goes wrong if you substitute it?
options: A 0.9 A stall is a legitimate operating state here, and a 1.0 A hold would trip on it
A lower hold rating drags the trip current down in proportion with it
The crowbar needs the higher hold rating before it can conduct fully

prompt: The servo rail never exceeds 5.5 V, so a 6.3 V capacitor looks like plenty. Why is C8 specified at 16 V?
options: Because a 1000 µF part is only made in ratings of 16 V and above
Because D3 clamps a transient at up to 10.3 V, and C8 is sitting on that node when it does
Because a higher voltage rating is what gives the part its low equivalent series resistance

prompt: You label J5 pin 2 as +5V rather than VSERVO. ERC passes without a word. What did that one keystroke do?
options: Nothing electrical: both names resolve to the same 5 V on this board
It leaves the servo unpowered, since +5V never reaches that connector
It puts the servo's stall current back through the USB cable and the logic fuse, rebuilding the brownout the board exists to prevent

prompt: To shorten a trace, someone moves F2 downstream of D2. What does that break?
options: The crowbar's deliberate short no longer runs through the fuse
Only cooling: a PTC away from the connector runs warmer than it should
Only trace length: the fuse guards the rail from either position

prompt: You install D2 the other way round, anode on the rail and cathode to ground. ERC passes. What happens at first power-up?
options: Nothing: a Schottky conducts either way at voltages this low
It protects better, since it now catches both fault polarities
It conducts on a perfectly correct supply, so the fuse trips every time you switch on

prompt: VSERVO needs 0.8 mm of copper and the Power class already sits at 0.5 mm. Why add a third net class instead of widening Power?
options: KiCad requires any net fed by a connector to sit in a class of its own
Only one net carries the amps, and Power also threads VBUS and 3V3 through tight space near the USB connector for a current that never arrives there
The servo rail is a different voltage from the logic rails, and one class cannot mix voltages

prompt: One 3 mm stretch of your VSERVO path came out at 0.25 mm, and DRC passes clean. Does it matter?
options: Yes: the whole 0.9 A goes through that section, so it runs hot while the rest of the rail is fine
No: DRC is the authority on trace width, and 0.25 mm is inside the fab's limits
No, as long as the average width along the whole rail stays above 0.8 mm

prompt: The servo cluster meets the ground plane at one deliberate point, at the bulk capacitor's ground. What does that prevent?
options: Extra vias, which the fab quotes and charges for individually
A DRC violation for a zone with more than one pad connection
The motor's switching return writing its own voltage across the copper the microcontroller uses as zero

prompt: On the viewer pass, which silkscreen text earns the most attention on this particular board?
options: The board name and revision, so the right file gets ordered
J4's polarity marks, J5's GND / V+ / SIG order, and C8's plus sign
The layer count in the corner, which the fab reads to set the stackup

prompt: You search the distributor for SS34 and add the first result to the cart. What is the risk?
options: You may get the SMA-package variant, a different part number that will not fit the pads you drew
Nothing: SS34 is one part, and the suffix only records the reel size
The price will beat the BOM, because the first result is usually a marketplace reseller

prompt: On a 1 A current-limited supply the servo dies mid-sweep while the serial console keeps ticking. What happened?
options: The board and the module together ate the headroom the servo needed
The supply sagged as it warmed, which is why larger bricks drift less
Start-up inrush reaches about 1.3 A, and the supply folded back right at that moment

prompt: D2 and D3 both carry a cathode band. What is assembly's job with them?
options: Point both bands at the input terminal, the way protection parts generally face
Match each band to its silkscreen mark before any heat lands on the pad
Nothing: on surface-mount diodes the band is a manufacturing mark rather than a polarity mark

prompt: On a freshly built board the meter beeps between VSERVO and VBUS. What does that beep mean?
options: A bridge has welded the two rails together, so the sag path this board removes is back
F2 has failed short, which is how a resettable fuse usually ends its life
Normal: the two rails share a ground, so the meter is reading the plane

prompt: You pinch the servo horn against a commanded move and the serial heartbeat never skips a line. What did that prove?
options: That the servo is weaker than its datasheet claims, so the stall stayed small
That the bulk capacitor carried the whole stall, which is what it is there for
The topology: worst-case motor current flowed and none of it crossed the logic path

prompt: Your finished board resets every time the servo starts a large move. What is the design-level suspect?
options: The PWM frequency is wrong, so the servo draws more than it should
The two rails are joined somewhere: a bridge or a mislabelled net has rebuilt the shared-rail failure
The USB port is too weak, and a wall charger will cure it
